title: Evaluating Knowledge Graph Accuracy Powered by Optimized Human-machine Collaboration

problem.claim: Evaluating the accuracy of an automatically constructed knowledge graph is challenging because it may contain many entities and triples.

gap.claim: Existing approaches evaluate triple accuracy associated with information extraction quality but ignore entity accuracy.

contributions.claim: An interactive human-machine method estimates both triple and entity accuracy with a statistical guarantee while reducing the overall evaluation cost.

A general annotation cost blends triples and entities generated from identical source text, and machines pre-compute and infer candidates for subsequent annotation rounds using speculative human feedback.
Monte Carlo Tree Search guides the annotation process by finding an approximate solution to the NP-hard triple order selection problem.

author_reported_evidence.claim: Extensive experiments reportedly show that the method uses less annotation cost while producing higher accuracy estimation quality than state-of-the-art approaches.

narrative_sequence.summary: Knowledge graph accuracy estimation is difficult at scale because automatically constructed graphs contain many entities and triples.
Knowledge graph construction involves information extraction and entity linking, but existing evaluation focuses on triples and ignores entities.
The method combines human verification with machine computation to estimate triple and entity accuracy under a statistical guarantee and uses a blended annotation cost.
Because annotation order selection is NP-hard, Monte Carlo Tree Search is used to find an approximate solution.
The authors report lower annotation cost and higher accuracy estimation quality than state-of-the-art approaches in extensive experiments.

source_observation.claim: The approach evaluates triples and entities jointly using a general annotation cost for items generated from identical source text.

interpretation.claim: Evaluation can be made more efficient when related quality dimensions share annotation context.

application.claim: For multi-stage extraction pipelines, design annotation workflows that jointly assess linked outputs originating from the same evidence.

exception.claim: The abstract does not establish whether this joint-cost design applies when outputs do not share source text.

source_observation.claim: Machine inference of future annotation candidates is combined with human verification, and Monte Carlo Tree Search addresses the NP-hard ordering problem.

interpretation.claim: Adaptive prioritization may reduce annotation effort when candidate selection is computationally difficult.

application.claim: Use feedback-informed candidate prioritization for human-in-the-loop evaluation workflows with costly review actions.

exception.claim: The abstract does not specify the approximation quality, computational overhead, or conditions under which the prioritization is beneficial.

unknowns: The statistical guarantee and estimator construction are not specified.
The annotation-cost function and machine inference procedure are not detailed.
The compared state-of-the-art approaches, datasets, metrics, and numerical results are not provided.
The approximation quality and computational cost of Monte Carlo Tree Search are not reported.
